content: The organization of trauma services, including the establishment of transfer criteria and arrangements between hospitals, has been shown to significantly reduce trauma-related mortality in regions that implement such systems. Evidence supporting this comes from panel reviews of preventable deaths, hospital trauma registry studies, and population-based research. Studies consistently demonstrate that improved trauma management systems lead to a reduction in mortality rates. For instance, panel reviews indicate a 50% decrease in medically preventable deaths following the implementation of trauma systems. Similarly, population-based studies and trauma registry analyses report a 15–20% or greater reduction in mortality in well-organized systems compared to less organized ones or the same systems prior to improvements. One notable study by Nathens et al. used population-based data to assess the impact of trauma system planning across all 50 U.S. states. Adjusting for confounding factors such as traffic laws and safety measures, they found an 8% reduction in overall trauma mortality in states with trauma systems. This figure includes individuals who died at the scene before receiving medical care. Importantly, the study highlighted that the benefits of trauma systems often become evident only after 10 years of implementation, reaching their peak effect at 16 years. When considering the relevance of these findings for developing countries, it is crucial to note that the observed improvements occurred in settings with similar resource levels. The trauma management systems required funding for enhanced organization and occasional additional resources to meet verification standards. The Essential Trauma Care Project aims to achieve similar organizational and planning improvements at a relatively low cost compared to the existing treatment systems. The project focuses on defining minimal, feasible standards applicable globally and reinforcing existing trauma care systems in diverse settings, including lowand middle-income countries. The authors of the project developed a list of medical goals to address the needs of injured patients, categorized into three main objectives: (1) treating life-threatening injuries promptly and effectively to maximize survival, (2) minimizing functional impairment from potentially disabling injuries to promote independence and community participation, and (3) reducing pain and psychological suffering. Specific medical goals include ensuring open airways, supporting impaired breathing, managing pneumothorax and hemothorax, controlling bleeding, treating shock with IV fluids, addressing traumatic brain injuries, repairing abdominal injuries, correcting extremity injuries, stabilizing spinal cord injuries, and providing appropriate rehabilitative services. Medications for these services and pain management should also be readily available. The implementation of these goals requires optimal use of human and physical resources. This includes ensuring that medical staff have the necessary training and skills, both through basic education and ongoing professional development, as well as maintaining the availability of essential equipment and supplies. Organizational mechanisms must be in place to replenish supplies and repair equipment promptly. These aspects are addressed in detail in the manual, which provides a resource matrix outlining the knowledge, skills, equipment, and supplies needed for various categories of trauma care, such as airway management, shock treatment, and rehabilitation. The guidelines emphasize that the provision of essential trauma services should not depend on a patient’s ability to pay. They also acknowledge the importance of integrating trauma care with other emergency medical services and broader healthcare systems. While the guidelines focus on facility-based trauma care, they recognize the critical role of pre-hospital care and mobile emergency medical services, particularly in rural areas where initial care is often provided by non-physician healthcare workers. The authors advocate for a collaborative, consensus-driven process involving clinicians, health ministry officials, and administrators to adapt and implement the guidelines at the national level. The ultimate goal of these guidelines is to enact improvements in trauma care processes that reduce mortality and disability. To monitor the success of these efforts, reliable and timely data on injury incidence and outcomes are essential, necessitating some form of surveillance. The guidelines also aim to ensure that the resources and expertise required for effective trauma care are available and integrated into the broader healthcare system. This includes addressing the needs of injured patients in diverse economic and geographic settings, with the expectation that these services will be accessible to all, regardless of financial means.
